title: Zero-copy returns
summary: Return a borrowed view (&str, &[T]) into the input instead of allocating a new value.
lecture: When the answer already exists inside the input - the first word of a string, a row of a matrix - you can return a slice pointing at it instead of copying it out. The signature says it all: fn first_word(input: &str) -> &str returns a view; -> String promises a fresh allocation every call.

Lifetime elision ties the borrowed return to the input automatically (one input reference → rule 2), and the borrow checker then guarantees the caller can't use the view after the input is gone. Zero cost, fully safe.

The reflex to train: before reaching for .to_string()/.to_owned() in a return position, ask whether the caller actually needs to OWN the result, or just to look at it. Owning is occasionally right (the value must outlive the input); viewing is the default.

example.caption: split_whitespace yields sub-slices - returning one costs nothing.
